title: Session 1: Python Basics
text: Today’s learning goals · Be able to read and write short Python programs (using variables, lists, loops, conditionals, and functions) which is genuinely all the Python an experiment needs.

title: Session 1: Python Basics
text:
Learning outcomes
After this session, you can:

Work in the Python environment on UCloud: open it, write code, run it, and read what the output (including error messages) tells you.
Create and inspect variables of different types, manipulate strings (.split(), .upper(), len()), format output with f-strings, and compare values (==, !=, <, >).
Build and modify lists: index, slice, append, remove, replace, and sort.
Write for loops to repeat an action over a list (i.e., the exact shape of an experiment’s trial loop (for each image: show it, record a response, give feedback)).
Use conditionals (if / elif / else) to make code respond differently to different inputs, including inside loops.
Define your own functions with parameters and return values: the tool that lets you write “show a stimulus, collect a response” once and call it 200 times.

title: Exercise 4 · Functions & modules
text:
Block 5 · Exercise for Block 5: Functions & modules. The last one of the day!
Same drill as the earlier exercises: try first, then the Hint, then Show the code. Work in the same .py file, with comments such as # Exercise 4 to keep it navigable.

title: Exercise 4 · Functions & modules
section: Part 1: Write your own simple function
text:
Part 1: Write your own simple function
Write a function that prints the expression this is my first function!, then call the function.






Hint





Define the function first (def, a name, parentheses, a colon, an indented body) — then call it by name, with parentheses.









🔒 Example code will be available here after the workshop

title: Exercise 4 · Functions & modules
text:
Part 2: Inputs & relational operators
Whew, we’ve gotten past that really basic exercise — let’s add layers:

Redefine the function with an input argument name.
Inside the function, evaluate whether the name is "anna".
If it is, print may be your teacher else print is not your teacher.
Call the function from the console, first passing your own name.
Then pass the name "anna".
What does your function print on each call?







Hint





Define the function with a parameter named name, then compare it with the string "anna". Remember which operator compares and which assigns.









🔒 Example code will be available here after the workshop

title: Exercise 4 · Functions & modules
text:
Part 3: Outputs & relational/logical operators
Now redefine the function, this time with an output:

Inside the function, define a variable called teacher with the value True if the input name is "anna", otherwise False.
Return this variable from the function.
Call the function with "anna" as input and store the returned value in a variable in the console.
Print that variable. What is it? And could you have gotten teacher from the console without the return?







Hint





Set teacher inside both branches of your if/else, and put return teacher at the end of the function — outside the if/else, but still inside the function. Indentation is doing the work here.









🔒 Example code will be available here after the workshop

title: Exercise 4 · Functions & modules
section: Part 4: Store your function in a module
text:
Part 4: Store your function in a module

Make a new .py file in the same folder as your exercise file. Name it my_module.py.
Copy your function from Part 3 into it and save.
In your exercise file, import the module with import my_module.
Call the function with my_module.first_function("anna") and store the returned value.
Print the returned value. Does it work?







Hint





Module name, dot, function name: my_module.first_function("anna"). If Python says ModuleNotFoundError, check the two files really are in the same folder and that the module is saved.









🔒 Example code will be available here after the workshop

title: Exercise 4 · Functions & modules
text:
Part 5: Get creative
Now the exciting part: run wild (not too wild). Make as many functions as you have time for, incorporating all of today’s concepts:

Variable types
Lists & loops (for loops, while loops)
Logical / relational operations
Function inputs & outputs
Modules

Store them in your module file, import it, call them. There are no right answers here, only correct syntax.
Stuck for inspiration? One suggestion that uses everything and that you will meet again next week in disguise: write word_lengths(text). Take a text as input, split() it into words, loop through them, and return a list with the number of letters in each word. Then feed it a sentence of your choice. (No solution for this but good practice for next week where a function with this exact shape shows a stimulus and collects a response, once per trial.)
Everything runs? That’s Session 1 complete. You now know variables, lists, loops, conditionals, and functions: genuinely all the Python an experiment needs. Next week we explore PsychoPy!

title: 5 · Logical operations
text: Block 4 · Understand relational and logical operators: the decision-making machinery behind every experiment.

title: 5 · Logical operations
text:
What is a relational operator?
We often want to write code that makes relational comparisons. A relational comparison assesses the relationship between two different values, such as whether one value is greater than, less than, or equal to another. Python has several built-in relational operators:
1 < 2    # Less than
1 > 2    # Greater than
1 <= 2   # Less than or equal to
1 >= 2   # Greater than or equal to
1 == 2   # Equal to
1 != 2   # Not equal to
True
False
True
False
False
True
Note the double equals: == compares, while a single = assigns. Mixing them up is one of the most common bugs in beginner code (Python will refuse to run if x = 1:, which is its way of protecting you).






🤔 Think first



Why do these relational comparisons return only True or False, never a number or a string?






Check your thinking





A relational comparison checks a single condition, and a condition can only hold or not hold: 1 < 2 is either true or it isn’t. There is no third option. This yes/no output is called a Boolean value, and it is exactly what if statements (below) run on.

title: 5 · Logical operations
text:
What is a logical operator?
Relational operators compare two values. Logical operators combine the results of multiple comparisons:
True and True    # and: True only when both sides are True.
True or False    # or: True when at least one side is True.
True != False    # xor: True when exactly one side is True.
>>> True
>>> True
>>> True
Now let’s put this into context. Predict all four before running:
x = 1
y = 2
z = 3

y > x and z > x           # both sides true?
y < x or z < x            # at least one side true?
(x == y) != (y > x)       # exactly one side true?
y > x and z > x and 10 > x  # operators can chain: every side must be true.

What do the four expressions return, in order?

Check the or line again — but also the xor: (x == y) is False and (y > x) is True. Are those results different from each other?


True, False, True, True.
The or line is False: it needs at least one true side, but y < x and z < x are both false. The xor line is True: False != True — the two conditions disagree, which is exactly what xor detects.








🤔 Think first



Why are there parentheses around the comparisons in the xor line, but not in the other logical operations?






Check your thinking





The parentheses make Python evaluate (x == y) and (y > x) first, then compare those two Boolean results with !=. Without them, Python reads x == y != y > x as one chained comparison — a different (and here, misleading) computation. When combining complete conditions, parentheses make your intention unambiguous — to Python and to the humans reading your code.

title: 5 · Logical operations
section: If statements: putting operators to work
text:
If statements: putting operators to work
Now, very excitingly, we can use operators inside if statements, which evaluate a condition and execute the code inside them only if the condition is met:
x = 1
y = 2
z = 3

# The indented code runs *only if* x < y evaluates to True.
if x < y:
    print(x < y)
>>> True
Here x is indeed less than y, so the condition holds and the code inside the statement runs. The syntax pattern (notice the colon and the indentation: same shape as loops):
if some_condition_that_is_true_or_false:
    code that runs ONLY when the condition is True
Because the indented code is executed only conditionally, if statements are called control flow statements: they control which code runs.

If–else statements
The final flourish for today. Suppose you want to run one line when a condition is true and a different line when it is not: enter if-else:
if x < y:
    print(f"{x} is less than {y}")
else:
    print(f"{x} is not less than {y}")  # runs *only* when the condition fails.
>>> 1 is less than 2
Note the colon after else and the indentation: the same syntax rules as if. We can of course use logical operators in the condition:
if x < y and x == 1:
    print(f"{x} is less than {y} and equals 1")
else:
    print(f"{x} is not both less than {y} and equal to 1")
>>> 1 is less than 2 and equals 1
Finally, conditions can have more than two branches. elif tests a new condition when the previous one failed, and statements can even be nested:
if x < 10:
    if x == 1:
        print("x is equal to 1")
    elif x == 2:
        print("x is equal to 2")
    else:
        print("x is less than 10 but not equal to 1 or 2")
else:
    print("x is 10 or more")

Suppose we set x = 2 and run the nested block. What prints?

True, 2 is less than 10, so we enter the outer block. But then the inner checks run: which one catches x = 2 first?


x is equal to 2: the outer if x < 10 passes, then the inner if x == 1 fails, so the elif x == 2 gets its turn and matches. Only one branch of an if/elif/else chain ever runs: the first one whose condition is True.



And a naming question: what does elif stand for in plain language?

Else if: test another condition, but only when the preceding if (or elif) came up False.








Summary



You have learned to perform basic Boolean operations. Operations that result in true-or-false output. Relational operators compare values; logical operators combine the Boolean results of two or more conditions. And if, if–else, elif and nested statements let those conditions control which code runs. In the PsychoPy sessions, this is precisely how feedback works: if the participant pressed the correct key, show the success image, else, show failure.


Predictions checked? Green sticky. Next: Functions.

title: 4 · Loops
text: Block 3 · Chapter follows Exercise 2. Understand basic for and while loops.

title: 4 · Loops
text:
What is a loop?
A loop is a programming structure that repeats a block of code. In this lesson you will meet the two common types:

For loops repeat code once for each item in a collection, such as a list.
While loops repeat code while a condition is true.

This is the single most important chapter of the day for what comes next: when we start learning PsychoPy, we’ll learn that an experiment is a loop: for each stimulus: show it, record a response, give feedback.

title: 4 · Loops
text:
For loops
Imagine you have five subject IDs and want to print each one. You could write a separate print() for every subject:
print("S01")
print("S02")
...
print("S05")
This becomes repetitive and difficult to update. Instead, store the IDs in a list and loop through the items:
subject_ids = ['S01', 'S02', 'S03', 'S04', 'S05']

for subject in subject_ids:
    print(subject)
>>> S01
>>> S02
>>> S03
>>> S04
>>> S05
In plain language: for every item in subject_ids, store that item in subject and print it. Notice the syntax: the for statement ends with a colon, and the next line is indented. That indented part is the body of the loop, and it runs once per item. Each repetition is called an iteration; during each one, subject temporarily holds the current ID.

Your turn. Using a list from Exercise 2: what does this print?
animals = ['cat', 'dog', 'owl']
for animal in animals:
    print(animal)

The loop variable holds one item at a time. Not the list, and not the word “animals”.


Three lines: cat, dog, owl; one iteration per item, one print per iteration.

title: 4 · Loops
text:
Looping by index
You can also loop through the index positions of a list. This is useful when you need both an item’s position and its value:
# Get the total number of subjects.
number_of_subjects = len(subject_ids)

# Create indices from 0 up to, but not including, number_of_subjects.
subject_index_range = range(number_of_subjects)

# Use each index to retrieve the corresponding subject ID.
for index in subject_index_range:
    print(f"Subject {index + 1}: {subject_ids[index]}")
Subject 1: S01
Subject 2: S02
Subject 3: S03
Subject 4: S04
Subject 5: S05
Look closely at index + 1: the indices run 0-4 (zero-indexed, as ever), but humans count subjects from 1, so we print index + 1 while using plain index for the lookup.

title: 4 · Loops
text:
Counter variables
Sometimes you need to update a number on every iteration. This number is called a counter variable — here counting how many days have been processed:
weekdays = ['monday', 'tuesday', 'wednesday', 'thursday', 'friday', 'saturday', 'sunday']

# Start a counter at zero.
day_of_week = 0

# Print each day, then add 1 to the counter.
for day in weekdays:
    print(f"The current day is {day}")
    day_of_week += 1
The current day is monday
The current day is tuesday
The current day is wednesday
The current day is thursday
The current day is friday
The current day is saturday
The current day is sunday
(+= 1 is shorthand for day_of_week = day_of_week + 1. Add one to what’s there.). Notice the syntax: the for statement ends with a colon, and the loop body must be indented.

After the loop finishes, we print the counter:
print(f"There are {day_of_week} days in the list.")
What exactly appears?

Careful. The counter started at 0, but it was incremented once for every item. How many increments happened?


There are 7 days in the list.. The counter went 0→7, one += 1 per iteration. Starting at 0 doesn’t mean ending one short: seven items, seven increments.

title: 4 · Loops
text:
While loops
While loops repeat a block of code while a condition is True. You will learn more about conditions in the logical-operations lesson. For now, read this example and predict before running:
day_of_week = 0

while day_of_week < 6:
    print(f"The current day is {weekdays[day_of_week]}")
    # Move to the next index so the condition will eventually become False.
    day_of_week += 1

Before you run it: how many lines does this print?

The condition is day_of_week < 6: strictly less than. Which values of the counter pass that test?


6 lines: monday through saturday. The counter values 0,1,2,3,4,5 pass the < 6 test; when it reaches 6, the condition is False and the loop stops before printing sunday. < versus <= is a one-character difference with a one-iteration consequence.


One warning while we’re here: the comment in the body is not decoration. If you forget the day_of_week += 1, the condition never becomes False — and the loop runs forever. It happens to everyone once; when it happens to you, click the console and press Ctrl-C to stop it.






Summary



Loops repeat code. Use a for loop to work through each item in a collection, and an index-based for loop when you also need each item’s position. A counter variable records progress by changing on every iteration. Use a while loop when repetition should continue only while a condition is True, and make sure something in the body eventually makes it False.


Predictions checked? Next: Exercise 3: Loops.

title: 3 · Lists
text: Block 3 · Chapter 4 of the day. Understand what a list is and how to use lists effectively.

title: 3 · Lists
text:
What are lists?
A list is, literally, a list of items, stored in order, that can be changed (lists are mutable, a word that will matter shortly). You define one with square brackets, items separated by commas:
variable_name = [item1, item2, item3]
Lists can contain items of the same type or of different types, and this is the data structure experiments run on: a list of stimuli, a list of responses, a list of reaction times.

title: 3 · Lists
text:
Making lists
You can create lists with all strings, all numeric data, or a combination:
# First, simple lists of same-type items.
shopping = ["apples", "pears", "bananas"]
test_scores = [90, 60, 100, 82]

# Now mixed items.
mixed_list = ["cats", 7, 309.45]

print(test_scores)
print(mixed_list)
>>> [90, 60, 100, 82]
>>> ['cats', 7, 309.45]
You can also put lists inside lists:
combined = [shopping, test_scores, mixed_list]
print(combined)
>>> [['apples', 'pears', 'bananas'], [90, 60, 100, 82], ['cats', 7, 309.45]]
Three items: each of which is itself a list. Keep that picture in mind for the prediction below.

title: 3 · Lists
text:
Indexing lists
We index lists just like we indexed character strings: square brackets after the name, index inside.
print(shopping[0])
print(shopping[1])
print(shopping[2])
apples
pears
bananas
You may recognise this syntax from the previous block. That’s because we were already working with lists when we used .split(): splitting a string returns a list, and everything you learned there (zero-indexing, negative indexing, two brackets for two levels) applies to all lists.

Sub-indexing, then: what does shopping[0][0:2] return?

That’s shopping[0]: the whole first item. The second bracket slices into that string: which characters does [0:2] take?


'ap': shopping[0] picks the string 'apples' out of the list, and [0:2] slices characters 0 and 1 out of that string. Stops before 2, as always.



And the list of lists: what does combined[1] give you?

Close if you answered 60, but count the brackets. One pair of brackets goes one level deep. What lives at position 1 of combined?


[90, 60, 100, 82] — the entire second list. combined’s items are whole lists, so one index retrieves a whole list. To reach 60 you’d go two levels: combined[1][1].

title: 3 · Lists
text:
Changing list items
Lists are mutable: we can change their contents after creating them. Remember upper(), which returned a new string and left the original untouched? Lists are the opposite. These operations change the list itself, in place. Three ways to do it:

Replace an item, using indexing.
Append an item to the end.
Insert an item at a chosen position.

Predict each print() before you run it. This is where the bracket-counting pays off. Our starting point:
print(shopping)
['apples', 'pears', 'bananas']
Replace the second item:
shopping[1] = "kiwi"
print(shopping)
['apples', 'kiwi', 'bananas']
Goodbye pears: index 1 is the second item. Now append:
shopping.append("raspberry")
print(shopping)
['apples', 'kiwi', 'bananas', 'raspberry']
append() always adds at the end. Finally, insert at a particular position:
shopping.insert(1, "blueberry")

The finale: what does print(shopping) show now? Type the full list.

Almost — insert(1, ...) puts the new item at index 1, and everything from there shifts right. Who ends up second?


['apples', 'blueberry', 'kiwi', 'bananas', 'raspberry']. insert(1, ...) places blueberry at index 1 and shifts kiwi, bananas and raspberry one step right. Nothing is overwritten. That’s the difference from shopping[1] = ..., which replaces.


In the PsychoPy sessions, these operations will become very familiar: stimuli is a list of image filenames, responses.append(key) collects what the participant pressed, and shuffling a list gives every participant their own trial order.
All predictions checked? Next: Exercise 2 — Lists.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text: Block 2 · Chapter 2 of 3 before the first break. Understand what a variable is in Python & the different types of variables.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
What is a variable?
A variable is a name we give to a value so we can store it and use it later in our code. The name stays the same, but the value stored in it can change while the program is running. A variable can store a number, a word, or a list of values.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Your first variable
Let’s create our first variable in Python. We will call it my_name and store a name in it.
my_name = "anna"
We can also add comments to explain what our code is doing. In Python, a comment starts with #. Everything after # on that line is ignored by Python.
# This variable stores my name.
my_name = "anna"
Now run the code by selecting it in your file and pressing Shift+Enter.
You will see the code executed in the console below. If you then type my_name on a new line and press Enter, Python will print the value stored in the variable:
>>> my_name = 'anna'
>>> my_name
'anna'
An easier way to see the output is to use the print() function:
# This variable stores my name.
my_name = "anna"

# This line prints the value stored in my_name.
print(my_name)
Select these lines and press Shift+Enter. You should see the value of my_name appear in the console.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Variable types
Python allows us to create variables that store different kinds of data. Today we will focus on some of the most common variable types.
We can find the type of a variable by using the type() function:
# Query the type of my_name.
type(my_name)
This returns <class 'str'>, which means that my_name is a string variable.

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Data Type 1: Regular string variables
String variables are defined by strings of characters. String variables are specified using single or double quotation marks around the string.
# If you use single quotes here, it won't work. Why?
dog_name_possessive = 'anna's dog's name is..'

# If you use double-quotes here it will work. 
dog_name_possessive = "anna's dog's name is.."






🤔 Think first



Why does the single-quoted version fail while the double-quoted version works?






Check your thinking





The apostrophe in anna’s ends the single-quoted string early. Python thinks the string stops after anna, and the rest is nonsense to it. Double quotes let Python see the apostrophe as just another character inside the string.






Indexing
Strings are stored like arrays of characters, meaning that you can individually access single characters in the string using indexing (square brackets around the indices you want to extract).
# Here you are indexing the first 4 characters in the variable my_name_possessive. 
# You use square brackets around the indices that you want to extract.
dog_name_possessive[0:4] # extract 4 characters from the 0th character.

# you can also count backwards from the end of a string using the minus sign, e.g.:
dog_name_possessive[-4:]
You may have noticed that we start indexing at 0 instead of 1. This is because Python is a zero-indexed language, so whenever you have a multi-item variable, the first item is always indexed using 0 instead of 1. CAREFUL: R is a 1-indexed langauge, so you always index the first item in a multi-item variable using 1 in R instead of 0.

Before you run it: what will dog_name_possessive[0:4] give you?

anna: characters 0, 1, 2 and 3. The index range [0:4] starts at 0 and stops before 4, so you get exactly 4 characters. (The console shows it wrapped in quotes ('anna') because it is a string.)

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
String methods
String variables have many built-in methods that we can call on them. Here are some useful string methods:

split()
If you type the name of your string variable followed by .split(), Python splits the string into smaller pieces, using the space character as the default delimiter. Try it in the console:
dog_name_possessive.split()
>>> ["anna's", "dog's", 'name', 'is..']
The split() method returns a list of strings. Each item is one part of the original text, separated by the chosen delimiter.
You can store the output in a variable, and since it is a list, you can index it, even down to characters within each item:
split_variable = dog_name_possessive.split()
split_variable[0]
split_variable[0][0]  # first letter of first word.
split_variable[1][1]  # second letter of second word.
>>> split_variable[0]
>>> "anna's"
>>> split_variable[0][0]  # first letter of first word.
>>> 'a'
>>> split_variable[1][1]  # second letter of second word.
>>> 'o'
So split_variable[1][1] means: take item 1 of the list ("dog's": remember, zero-indexed!), then character 1 of that string.
You can also use split() with a different delimiter, such as an underscore:
subject_id = "S_01"
subject_id.split("_")
>>> ['S', '01']

Given responses = "left right left left", what does responses.split() return?

['left', 'right', 'left', 'left']: a list of four strings, one per word. Repeats are kept; split() just cuts, it doesn’t deduplicate.



Given date = "2026-09-14", what does date.split("-") return?

The delimiter is the cut line. It doesn’t survive into the pieces.


['2026', '09', '14']. Three pieces, dashes gone. Note they are strings, not numbers: '09' keeps its leading zero, and you couldn’t do maths with it without converting first.




upper()
The upper() method converts all letters in a string to uppercase.
name = "anna"
name.upper()
>>> 'ANNA'
Note that upper() does not change name itself — it returns a new, uppercased string. If you want to keep it, store it:
name_upper = name.upper()
print(name_upper)
>>> ANNA
# or store the result in a new variable.
name_upper = name.upper()
print(name_upper)
Here are a few more useful string methods:
word = " subject_01 "
print(word.lower())
print(word.strip())
print(word.replace("p", "P"))
print(word.startswith(" "))
print(word.endswith(" "))


len()
And, finally, we can get the length of a string variable using len() (not a string-specific method)
len(word)
>>> 12
The 10 characters of subject_01 plus the two spaces. Invisible characters count, which is exactly why .strip() exists.
There’s lots more that you can do with strings, but these are the basics!

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Data Type 2: Regular numeric variables
Now let’s turn to our other fundamental variable type: numeric. There are two basic numeric types:

Integers: whole numbers (no decimal point)
Floating points: numbers with a decimal point

# This is an integer.
a = 1
type(a)
>>> int
# This is a floating point.
b = 1.5
type(b)
>>> float
c = 1.00

c stores the value one, but what does type(c) return? float or int?

<class 'float'>: a floating point. The value is a whole number, but writing it with a decimal point makes it a float. What matters is how it is written, not what it equals.


The same logic applies to operations:
# What happens when you combine types in operations?
d = b + c
type(d)
>>> float
Adding the float b to the float c gives a float — d is 2.5. And even when an operation on two floats produces a whole number, the result stays a floating point:
e = 1.5 + 1.5
type(e)
print(e)
<class 'float'>
3.0
The value is three — but Python shows it as 3.0: the .0 is the float’s badge. It never silently becomes an integer.
Standard numeric operations are addition (shown above), subtraction, multiplication and division:
print(a - b)   # subtraction
print(a * b)   # multiplication
print(a / b)   # division
-0.5
1.5
0.6666666666666666

title: 2 · Basics: Variables & variable types
text:
Printing variables with f-strings
Imagine that you want to print reaction times for a given subject on an experiment screen. The subject is different in each experiment, and so is their reaction time.
You can create a special expression called an f-string, where you embed variables inside a string: start the string with f, then place variable names inside curly brackets {}.
subject_id = "S_01"
reaction_time = 0.45
message = f"Reaction time for {subject_id}: {reaction_time:.2f} seconds"
Here {subject_id} inserts the value of the subject ID variable, and {reaction_time:.2f} inserts the value of reaction_time, where .2f formats the number with two digits after the decimal point.

What exactly does print(message) show?

Reaction time for S_01: 0.45 seconds: the curly-bracket parts are replaced by the variables’ values, and everything else is printed as-is. In Session 2, messages like this become the text you show on the experiment screen.


All predictions checked? Next: Exercise 1 — Variables & data types.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text: Welcome! Over the coming workshop sessions, you’ll go from typing your very first line of Python to watching a full behavioural experiment run on your own screen: window, stimuli, responses, feedback, the lot. Between you and that moment stand a handful of Python concepts and a few dozen extremely fixable error messages. We assume no programming experience. If you can rename a file, you’re qualified to start.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
Why programming?
Nearly every empirical experiment in cognitive science (e.g. reaction-time studies, reading paradigms, eye-tracking, EEG) is implemented in code. A working knowledge of Python allows you to build precisely the experiment your research question requires, to understand the structure and provenance of your data, and to diagnose problems when they arise.
The aim of these three sessions is a modest form of fluency: by the end, the experiment running on your screen should be a system you can read, modify, and reason about. These skills will hopefully outlast the course: designing, implementing, and troubleshooting your own experiments is part of the everyday craft of working scientists, in cognitive science and well beyond.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
Why Python and not R?
The Python programming language is optimal for coding experiments because it has a special library called PsychoPy for doing so.
In contrast, the R programming language is optimal for statistical analyses, as it was designed specifically for this purpose.
Therefore, this workshop on programming for experiments focuses on Python instead of R, which you instead cover in your Methods 1 practical classes.
However, as you will learn over the course of the semester, many of the programming concepts that we cover in Session 1 are generalizable to R and all other languages.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
The three sessions
Session 1 · Python basics Variables, lists, loops, conditionals, functions. These are the handful of building blocks that all programs are made of. Everything you learn here gets used directly in Session 2.
[Session 2 · Introduction to PsychoPy] (materials coming) PsychoPy is the Python library psychologists use to run experiments: it opens windows, draws stimuli, and records keypresses with precise timing. You build an experiment step by step and leave with a script that runs: images in random order, keyboard responses, feedback on every trial, and more..
Session 3 · From cogwheels to words (materials coming) Swap the images for words, add a clock and a logfile, and your CogWheel script becomes a self-paced reading experiment, the direct starting point for your Portfolio 2 prototype.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
How the sessions work
Each session follows the same rhythm: a short lecture introduces the concepts and demonstrates them live, and you then put them to work in a set of exercises you complete on your own, at your own pace, with the teaching team circulating. Three habits will serve you well throughout:

Predict before you run. Whenever you see a 🔮 Predict first box, write down what the code will do before running it.
Run constantly. Run your code after every small change, not after twenty lines. Small steps make bugs easy to find.
Never stay stuck. Ten minutes on the same bug is the signal to ask: check the error message, unfold the solution, or wave a teacher over. Sitting silently with a bug is the one wrong way to use these sessions.

title: Programming experiments: Python x PsychoPy
text:
What you need

Your own laptop with PsychoPy installed. Install instructions are sent out before Session 2, and each session starts with a setup check. If the install fights back, come 15 minutes early.
Curiosity. A willingness to try things, break things, and read the occasional error message will carry you further than any prior experience would.

Ready? Start with Session 1.

Create your first Python code file
You can now create a new Python code file. Here’s how:

“Hello world!”: Run your first line of Python code
In your new code file, enter your first line of Python code:
print("Hello world!")

Your first prediction! Throughout these sessions, boxes like this ask you to guess what code will do before you run it. That’s where the learning happens, and wrong guesses are very welcome and encouraged. After a few tries the box will offer to show you the answer, so you can never get stuck. So: what exactly will appear in the console when this line runs? Take a guess.

Hello world!. Note that there are no quotation marks. The quotes tell Python where the text starts and ends; they are not part of the text itself.

title: 6 · Functions & modules
text: Block 5 · How to write your own function.

title: 6 · Functions & modules
text:
What is a function?
A function is like a recipe: it contains instructions that run when you call it by name.
Let’s say we want to make a Python function that prints “This is a greeting” every time it runs. We will call the function greeting. First, the definition syntax:
def function_name():
     # instructions go here
Let’s now try defining the function greeting:
# Define the function.
def greeting():
     print("This is a greeting")
Once Python has evaluated the definition, the function can be called by name and its contents will execute.
greeting()
This calls the function and the output should be:
This is a greeting
Note that running the definition printed nothing. The body only runs when the function is called.

title: 6 · Functions & modules
section: Everything that happens inside a function stays inside a function (unless otherwise specified)
text:
Everything that happens inside a function stays inside a function (unless otherwise specified)
Let’s define variables inside the function greeting:
def greeting():
    casual = "hey"
    formal = "hello"

    print(casual)
    print(formal)
And now call the function:
greeting()
hey
hello

Now type casual into the console and press Enter. What happens?

Would Python know what casual is out here? Where was it created?


A NameError: Python does not know casual out here, because it was created inside the function. By default, variables created inside functions have local scope: they can only be accessed from inside that function.

title: 6 · Functions & modules
text:
Function outputs and inputs
Although local variables cannot normally be accessed outside a function, the return statement sends values back to the code that called the function. Let’s return both casual and formal from greeting:
def greeting():
    casual = "hey"
    formal = "hello"

    print(casual)
    print(formal)

    return casual, formal
Now we can call the function and store its returned values in variables:
# Store the returned values in two separate variables.
casual_greeting, formal_greeting = greeting()

# Store both returned values in one tuple.
greeting_types = greeting()
In the first case, the two returned values are unpacked into two separate variables. In the second case, both values are stored in a tuple. A tuple is like a list, but its values cannot be changed. It is indexed the same way as a list: greeting_types[0] and greeting_types[1].
We can also pass inputs to functions. Imagine that we want greeting to print either a casual or a formal greeting depending on our relationship with the person being greeted. We can pass that information as an input.
def greeting(relation_to_greeted_person):
    casual = "hey"
    formal = "hello"

    if relation_to_greeted_person == "friend":
        print(casual)
        return casual
    else:
        print(formal)
        return formal
Now call the function with an input value. Inside the function, that value is stored in relation_to_greeted_person:
greeting_type = greeting("friend")
print(greeting_type)
>>> hey  # printed inside the function
>>> hey  # printed by print(greeting_type)
Two heys: one printed inside the function, one by our print(greeting_type). The function both printed and returned.
We can pass multiple input arguments too:
def greeting(relation_to_greeted_person, name):
    casual = "hey"
    formal = "hello"

    if relation_to_greeted_person == "friend":
        print(f"{casual} {name}!")
        return casual
    else:
        print(f"{formal} {name}!")
        return formal
greeting_type = greeting("friend", "anna")
hey anna!

The call printed hey anna!. But what value is now stored in greeting_type? (Check the return line before answering.)

hey anna! is what got printed, but look at what the function returns. Are they the same thing?


hey: the function returns casual, not the personalised f-string it printed. What a function shows and what it hands back are independent, and only the returned value lands in the variable. (And note: assigning a return value does not display it. To see it, print(greeting_type) explicitly.)

title: 6 · Functions & modules
text:
Modules
Functions can become lengthy, and it can be inconvenient to define every function in the main code file for a project. To keep your code organized, you can store function definitions in a separate Python file: a .py file containing reusable code is called a module, and it works like a small library of functions.
To use a function from a module, import the module where you are working:
# In greeting_types.py:
def greetings():
    print("Hello, world!")
After creating greeting_types.py and defining greetings() there, import the module in the console or another Python file:
import greeting_types

greeting_types.greetings()
Hello, world!
The pattern is module name, dot, function: greeting_types.greetings().






Summary



Functions are reusable recipes that can accept inputs and return outputs, and what they print is not what they return. Variables inside them are local. Modules are Python files that help organize and reuse functions, unlocked with import.


Lesson learned? Next: Exercise 4: Putting it all together — Logical operations & functions.
